Volume 10 · Chapter 10

Numerical pricing and Monte Carlo

A pricing program should return evidence about its error as well as a number. By the end of this chapter you should be able to implement a recombining tree, a stable finite-difference scheme and a simulation estimator; distinguish the errors each introduces; and evaluate an exercise rule without giving it information from the future.

Prerequisites are the finite-market replication and stopping arguments in Chapter 6, Brownian motion and GBM in Chapter 7, the dividend-adjusted PDE and vanilla expectation in Chapter 8, and sensitivities and inverse conditioning in Chapter 9. Probability laws, confidence intervals and elementary numerical analysis come from Volumes 2–3. Prices below are currency units (CU) per option; time is measured in years. Every numerical case is authored synthetic data.

1. Specify the target before measuring error

Suppose a desk receives a put price of 11.59 and an estimated standard error of 0.09. Does this establish accuracy to a few cents? Only if we know what was computed. A European payoff, an option exercisable on quarterly dates, and a continuously exercisable American claim have different values even under the same stock model. Exact sampling of a terminal stock does not sample its intervening maximum. A narrow confidence interval around a misspecified model does not repair the model.

For a fixed pricing probability Q, constant rate r and payoff H, the European target is V = EQ[e−rTH]. In this chapter Q makes an ex-dividend stock satisfy dS = (r − q)S dt + σS dW, with constant yield q. Under a chosen model, let VD be a target with a finite monitoring/exercise convention D, VD,h,L its numerical approximation with mesh h and spatial cutoff L, and V̂ its sample estimate. The exact identity

V̂ − V = (VD − V) + (VD,h,L − VD) + (V̂ − VD,h,L)

separates contractual/grid approximation, deterministic numerical error and sampling error. Boundary truncation and floating-point error can be separated further. Differences between the chosen stochastic model and executable prices are another question; they are not one more known term in a confidence interval. A contract defined on D has no monitoring approximation error relative to its own definition.

A useful test changes one component at a time: refine time with space fixed; enlarge the domain at comparable resolution; change the random seed while fixing the algorithm; compare independent methods for the same European claim; and inspect exercise dates under unchanged transitions. With a local vega lower bound ν ≥ νmin > 0 throughout an implied-volatility bracket, the mean-value theorem gives |δσ| ≤ |δV|/νmin. Thus a price tolerance is not a universal volatility tolerance. A finite-difference Greek also amplifies price errors: for central gamma with price errors bounded by ε, the numerator's error is at most 4ε, giving 4ε/(ΔS)2. Making the bump smaller can make that part worse.

2. Recombining trees and honest refinement

Let Δt = T/N, u = exp(σ√Δt), d = 1/u and Si,j = S0ujdi−j, where j counts up moves. The Cox–Ross–Rubinstein construction uses

p = [e(r−q)Δt − d]/(u − d),   D = e−rΔt,   Vi,j = D[(1 − p)Vi+1,j + pVi+1,j+1].

The strict no-arbitrage condition is d < e(r−q)Δt < u. An invalid p is a failed model input, not a probability to clip. For q = 0 this is Chapter 6's stock/account hedge. With continuously reinvested proportional dividends, buy Δe−qΔt shares at the node: reinvestment makes that Δ shares at the next date. Solving the two terminal equations with cash and that position produces the stated p. The tree describes interval transitions and this dividend convention; it does not specify a continuously traded diffusion between nodes.

The terminal array contains g(SN,j). Sweep backward, overwriting an array of length N + 1, for O(N2) work and O(N) storage. For a European payoff an independent implementation can instead use the binomial sum DNΣj C(N,j)pj(1 − p)N−jg(SN,j). Avoid giant factorials and subtracting nearly equal exponentials; the lab uses expm1 for p. Binomial weights can be built recursively or in logarithms at larger N.

The one-step stock mean is exactly Se(r−q)Δt. If ξ is the log increment ±σ√Δt, expansion gives p = 1/2 + [(r − q − σ2/2)/(2σ)]√Δt + O(Δt3/2), Eξ = (r − q − σ2/2)Δt + O(Δt2) and Var ξ = σ2Δt + O(Δt2). These explain the diffusion target. They alone do not prove convergence of option prices or stopping boundaries: a limit theorem plus payoff integrability is required, and exercise requires more than terminal weak convergence. We do not prove general tree convergence here. The proved error theorem below concerns a declared PDE scheme. Tree tables are numerical evidence against a known European benchmark, with no universal rate inferred.

Finite exercise and the Snell recursion

For permitted node dates A containing N, define VN = gN and at earlier nodes

Ci = D EQ[Vi+1 | Fi],   Vi = max(gi, Ci) if i ∈ A;   Vi = Ci otherwise.

Proof. On a finite tree, any admissible stopping time either exercises now or continues. Its continuation conditional value is no greater than Ci if Vi+1 already dominates every future rule. This is true at maturity, so backward induction gives domination at every node. Exercise on the first permitted node with gi ≥ Ci, and otherwise follow the inductively optimal rule. This uses only current information and attains the maximum. Thus the recursion equals the maximum discounted expected receipt over all stopping times on A. All expectations are finite here; equality can be resolved consistently in favor of exercise.

If A ⊆ A′ within the same tree and filtration, every A-rule is feasible on A′, so V(A) ≤ V(A′). Changing N in CRR changes u, d, p and the entire law, so this comparison does not imply that successive CRR American estimates are monotone. Calling every node “American” abbreviates an all-grid-date claim, not a theorem about continuous exercise. A pathwise hindsight maximum E[maxi∈ADigi] is an upper bound because it dominates each feasible receipt pathwise, but it usually chooses using information unavailable at the exercise date.

Worked example 1: an exercise decision that changes the price

Take a two-period non-dividend tree with S0 = 80, u = 5/4, d = 4/5, per-period account factor R = 26/25 and put strike 84. Then p = (26/25 − 4/5)/(5/4 − 4/5) = 8/15. Maturity stocks ordered down/down, mixed, up/up are 51.2, 80 and 125, so payoffs are 32.8, 4 and 0.

At date 1 the down node has stock 64 and continuation [(7/15)32.8 + (8/15)4]/1.04 = 218/13 ≈ 16.769231. Immediate exercise gives 20, so exercise. The up node has stock 100, intrinsic zero and continuation [(7/15)4]/1.04 = 70/39 ≈ 1.794872, so continue. European root value is 12845/1521 ≈ 8.445102; all-date value is [(7/15)20 + (8/15)(70/39)]/1.04 = 15050/1521 ≈ 9.894806. Immediate root exercise gives only 4. The premium 2205/1521 ≈ 1.449704 is the value of an informed date-1 decision, not an estimated physical return.

3. A finite-difference method with a proved error statement

Set remaining time τ = T − t, log coordinate x = log(S/Sref) and w(τ,x) = erτV(T − τ,Srefex). The chain rule S VS = Vx, S2VSS = Vxx − Vx turns the Black–Scholes PDE into

wτ = a wxx + b wx,   a = σ2/2 > 0,   b = r − q − σ2/2.

Choose x ∈ [−L,L], xj = −L + jh, h = 2L/M, time step k = T/n and prescribed boundary functions. Initial data for a put are (K − Srefex)+. For interior j, forward time and central space give

Wjm+1 = αWj−1m + βWjm + γWj+1m,
α = k(a/h2 − b/(2h)),   β = 1 − 2ak/h2,   γ = k(a/h2 + b/(2h)).

Here β is a scheme coefficient; the control-variate coefficient introduced later will be called βc. We require |b|h ≤ 2a and 2ak/h2 ≤ 1. Then all three weights are nonnegative and sum to one. The first restriction controls central differencing of drift; reducing time alone cannot fix its violation. The second is the explicit time-step restriction. Giles's finite-difference lecture supplies a primary introduction to the heat-equation stencil and stability; the drift, discount transformation and error bounds here are derived explicitly.

Maximum principle, perturbation bound and consistency

Discrete theorem. Under the two restrictions, every interior update is a convex combination. Therefore nonnegative initial/boundary data remain nonnegative, and the entire space-time solution lies between the minimum and maximum of those data. If two solutions differ by at most ε on all initial and prescribed boundary nodes, then their difference is at most ε everywhere. Proof: apply the convex-combination inequality to the difference at each step, and induct; new boundary values also satisfy the bound. This is a maximum-norm stability result, including boundary errors. For prices, multiply the final w-error by e−rT; negative r is allowed and increases that factor.

Now suppose an exact solution w on the closed rectangle has continuous derivatives wττ, wxxx, wxxxx and the derivatives needed by the PDE. Let their absolute suprema be Mtt, M3 and M4. Taylor's theorem with integral remainders bounds the one-step residual of its grid samples by kη, where

η = (k/2)Mtt + (a h2/12)M4 + (|b|h2/6)M3.

Indeed the forward time quotient differs from wτ by at most kMtt/2, the symmetric second difference differs from wxx by h2M4/12, and the symmetric first difference differs from wx by h2M3/6. Subtract the numerical update from the exact residual equation. If Em is the largest nodal error through time m, the convex weights and residual imply Em+1 ≤ max(ε,Em + kη), with ε bounding initial and all boundary errors. Induction yields

maxj|Wjn − w(T,xj)| ≤ ε + Tη.

Thus, on this fixed domain with the stated smooth solution, consistent initial/boundary data and stable refinements, the method converges at O(k + h2). This is a theorem with an explicit error source, not a rate fitted to three numbers. Add T times a bounded per-unit-time implementation residual to account for bounded rounding perturbations; the theorem itself uses real arithmetic and does not estimate that floating-point bound automatically.

A vanilla payoff has a kink at τ = 0 and does not satisfy these closed-rectangle smoothness assumptions. Smoothing for positive τ does not by itself bound the derivatives uniformly down to zero. Consequently this proof does not certify the advertised rate for the raw put initialization. The lab verifies the theorem on the manufactured smooth solution w = exp(κx + (aκ2 + bκ)τ), κ = 1.3, and separately compares the actual put to an analytic oracle. Payoff averaging, implicit startup steps and weak-solution convergence theory are useful extensions, not conclusions proved here.

The boundary is part of the numerical problem

A finite interval is not the full stock domain. For the verification experiment, use the exact vanilla put value at Slow and Shigh at each remaining time, multiplied by erτ. This deliberately isolates mesh error and would not solve an unknown exotic's boundary problem. A practical alternative uses w(τ,−L) ≈ max(K − Slowe(r−q)τ,0) and w(τ,L) ≈ 0. These are approximations at finite positive stock values, even if their economic asymptotes are correct.

On an identical mesh, the maximum discrepancy εB between these two supplied boundary arrays bounds the difference of the two numerical solutions by εB. The lab reports e−rTεB as a discrete boundary-effect bound. It is not a continuum domain-truncation certificate or a total pricing-error bound. Enlarging L without increasing M coarsens h and can worsen mesh error. A stability check must be rerun after every parameter or grid change.

An implicit backward-time update solves (I − kLh)Wm+1 = Wm, usually via a tridiagonal system. When the same spatial off-diagonal coefficients are nonnegative, its matrix has positive diagonal and strict row diagonal dominance by 1; a discrete-minimum argument gives inverse positivity. At a negative minimum of a vector z with nonnegative boundary values, (I − kLh)z has a negative component, so it cannot equal a nonnegative right side. This explains why implicit methods avoid the explicit time restriction. It does not remove drift resolution, boundary error or the need to solve the system accurately. Crank–Nicolson averages explicit and implicit time operators; its often-quoted stability does not guarantee positivity for a coarse step. We implement only the explicit method here.

Worked example 2: a smooth theorem and a kinked payoff

The main lab uses S = 96, K = 100, r = .04, q = .015, σ = .25, T = 1.5. Thus a = .03125 and b = −.00625. With L = 1.6, M = 40 and n = 100, h = .08 and k = .015. The weights are (.073828125, .853515625, .07265625): positive, summing to one. Halving h and quartering k preserves the diffusion weight while reducing the drift weight.

For the manufactured exponential, set θ = aκ2 + bκ. Its maximum on the rectangle is A = exp(κL + max(θT,0)); hence Mtt = θ2A, M3 = κ3A and M4 = κ4A. Exact initial/boundary data give ε = 0. The theorem's error bounds on (M,n) = (40,100), (80,400), (160,1600) are .000991509, .000247877 and .0000619693. Actual maximum nodal errors are approximately .000122256, .0000306572 and .00000767936, all below their bounds.

The analytic European put is 11.596767761. With exact boundary values the same three option grids give 11.612615536, 11.578416115 and 11.592656262. Their signed errors are +.015847775, −.018351645 and −.004111499. The first refinement makes the absolute error larger because alignment of the payoff kink also changes. We cannot transplant the manufactured solution's rate or claim monotonic improvement. The last grid is useful evidence, not a certified four-decimal option value.

4. Monte Carlo: what randomness estimates

For a European GBM claim, draw Z ∼ N(0,1) and set ST = S exp[(r − q − σ2/2)T + σ√T Z]. This is the exact transition law of the stated diffusion, so no Euler time-discretization bias enters a terminal payoff. For a claim monitored at several dates, use independent normal increments and this exact conditional transition on each interval. That is exact for the selected dates, not for an unobserved continuous barrier. Under a general SDE, Euler or another scheme adds approximation error requiring a separate analysis.

Let Yi = e−rTg(ST(i)) be iid with mean V and variance v < ∞. Linearity and independence give EȲ = V and Var(Ȳ) = v/n. The unbiased sample variance is s2 = Σ(Yi − Ȳ)2/(n − 1), since expanding around V gives EΣ(Yi − Ȳ)2 = nv − nv/n = (n − 1)v. The finite-variance CLT and consistency of s2, established in the probability volume, yield the approximate 95% interval Ȳ ± 1.959964 s/√n when v > 0. It is a fixed-sample large-sample statement, not exact coverage at every n or under arbitrary repeated stopping. A rare-event sample can contain only zeros and report s = 0 even when the true variance is positive; zero estimated error is not proof of a zero-valued claim. Haugh's output-analysis notes discuss this sampling framework and run-length planning.

For a put, 0 ≤ Y ≤ B = Ke−rT, even if r < 0. A finite-sample alternative is

P(|Ȳ − V| ≥ ε) ≤ 2 exp(−2nε2/B2),   εα = B√[log(2/α)/(2n)].

Bound proof. For any X ∈ [0,B], let ψ(λ) = log E exp[λ(X − EX)]. Boundedness permits differentiation; ψ″(λ) is the variance under the tilted distribution. Any variable in [0,B] has variance at most B2/4 because Var X = mincE(X − c)2 ≤ E(X − B/2)2 ≤ B2/4. Since ψ(0) = ψ′(0) = 0, integration gives ψ(λ) ≤ λ2B2/8 for either sign of λ. Independence multiplies moment-generating functions. Markov's inequality gives P(Ȳ − V ≥ ε) ≤ exp[−λnε + nλ2B2/8]; minimizing at λ = 4ε/B2 and applying the same reasoning to −X proves the two tails. No normal approximation is involved. The bound is usually conservative.

The lab fixes the sample size in advance. Its authored deterministic test stream hashes the ASCII text v10-c10:seed:index with SHA256, uses the first two 64-bit words' top 53 bits to form positive midpoint uniforms, then applies Box–Muller. In ideal arithmetic, independent continuous uniforms U,V produce Z1 = √(−2log U)cos(2πV), Z2 = √(−2log U)sin(2πV): in polar coordinates the radial density ρe−ρ²/2 and uniform angle give joint density exp[−(z12 + z22)/2]/(2π). The program is deterministic and finite precision; hashing plus a seed is not a proof of independent uniforms or calibrated interval coverage. The continuous-normal formulas are analytical reference targets. A few moment checks can reveal mistakes but cannot certify a random generator.

5. Variance reduction must preserve the target

For a payoff function f with E[f(Z)2] < ∞ and symmetric normal Z, the antithetic observation A = [f(Z) + f(−Z)]/2 has the same mean as f(Z). With n independent pairs,

Var(Ā) = [Var(f(Z)) + Cov(f(Z),f(−Z))]/(2n).

Compare this with 2n independent payoff evaluations, whose mean variance is Var(f(Z))/(2n). A put's f is decreasing, while f(−z) is increasing. For independent copies Z,Z′,

2 Cov(g(Z),h(Z)) = E[(g(Z) − g(Z′))(h(Z) − h(Z′))].

Opposite monotonicity makes the product nonpositive, proving nonpositive covariance and no increase in variance at this equal payoff count. Constant or degenerate payoffs can give equality. General nonmonotone payoffs need not improve: f(z) = z2 makes both members identical and doubles the variance relative to 2n independent draws. Estimate the standard error across the n pair means, not by falsely treating the 2n dependent members as independent. Wall-clock efficiency also depends on cost per observation.

A control variate uses a random variable X with known expectation m. For a fixed coefficient βc, define Yc = Y − βc(X − m). Then

EYc = EY,   Var(Yc) = Var Y + βc2Var X − 2βcCov(Y,X).

When Var X > 0, completing the square gives βc* = Cov(Y,X)/Var X and minimum variance Var Y − Cov(Y,X)2/Var X. The covariance inequality ensures this is nonnegative. A wrong sign or poor coefficient can increase variance. If β̂ is fitted on independent pilot data, conditional on that pilot the main-sample mean still has expectation EY; apply the variance analysis conditionally to the frozen coefficient. Fitting and evaluating on the same observations destroys this simple unbiasedness argument because E[β̂(X̄ − m)] need not be zero. The lab uses a predeclared coefficient and never estimates it from its evaluation sample. Haugh's variance-reduction notes offer further worked methods; this chapter supplies its own proofs and examples.

For a put choose X = e−rTST, m = Se−qT. The discounted stock's variance is m2(eσ²T − 1). Let Lj = E[STj1{ST < K}], j = 0,1,2. Completing the Gaussian square as in Chapter 8 gives

Lj = Sjej(r−q)T+j(j−1)σ²T/2 Φ({log(K/S) − [r − q + (j − 1/2)σ²]T}/[σ√T]).

With D = e−rT, EY = D(KL0 − L1), EY2 = D2(K2L0 − 2KL1 + L2) and EYX = D2(KL1 − L2). These provide independent analytical moment targets and the coefficient's sign. The control-adjusted variable is generally unbounded because X is; the put's bounded-payoff Hoeffding formula cannot simply be reused. Nor is the coefficient optimal for raw observations necessarily optimal after antithetic pairing: both covariance and control variance change.

Worked example 3: a reduction that becomes an increase when combined

For the main case, the analytical put mean is 11.596767761, Var Y ≈ 201.134519, Var X ≈ 865.938555 and Cov(Y,X) ≈ −331.997470. Thus βc* ≈ −.383396. Predeclare βc = −.35, giving Var Yc ≈ 74.813763. At 8192 iid observations the ideal standard errors are about .156693 raw and .095564 controlled. Both estimate the same expectation.

The supplied seed produces the following reproducible diagnostics. The raw and fixed-control methods use 8192 observations; the antithetic methods use 4096 independent pair units, each requiring two payoff evaluations.

EstimatorEstimateEstimated standard errorApproximate 95% interval
Plain11.561078.156430[11.254481, 11.867675]
Fixed control −.3511.601719.095051[11.415421, 11.788016]
Antithetic pair means11.558921.091724[11.379146, 11.738695]
Antithetic plus the same control11.557247.123413[11.315361, 11.799133]

Adding this raw-observation control to the pair means makes their estimated variance worse. This is not inconsistent with the optimal-control theorem: the coefficient was optimized for neither the paired covariance nor the paired control variance. A separate pilot or analytical paired moments would be required. The bounded put's 95% Hoeffding half-width is 1.413122 for 8192 raw observations and 1.998456 for 4096 pair observations; it ignores the actual variance reduction and is much wider. No interval in this table covers model error, and a single successful seed is not a coverage experiment.

6. Simulation and early exercise: learn a rule, then evaluate it

At a finite exercise date, the correct continuation is a conditional expectation given the current state or sufficient payoff history. Averaging each path's future maximum substitutes foresight. One practical approach approximates continuation by basis functions of current information. On training paths, work backward: regress discounted future cash flows from the currently selected later policy on φ1(state), …, φk(state); store coefficients; exercise when immediate payoff exceeds the fitted continuation. Include relevant path history for Asian or barrier claims. A stock price alone need not be Markov for the contract.

Freeze every coefficient and tuning choice before generating independent evaluation paths. For fixed training data A, the resulting evaluation rule τA is a stopping time provided its decision at date i uses only that date's information. Therefore

E[e−rτAg(τA) | A] ≤ Vgrid.

This inequality follows directly from the supremum over feasible rules. Averaging over A preserves it. The held-out mean is unbiased for the selected rule's value conditional on A; its expectation is a lower bound for the optimal finite-grid value. An individual estimate can exceed Vgrid because of sampling noise. This is not a proof of regression consistency, near-optimality or convergence to a continuously exercisable claim. Independent policy evaluation is central to the simulation approach discussed by Haugh's primary paper on duality and simulation; dual upper bounds and full regression theory are further study.

The evaluation sample must remain separate from selecting bases, exercise thresholds or the “best” of many seeds. Otherwise it has become training data. If a report chooses the largest of several noisy policy values on its test set, that selection creates optimism even when each fixed-policy estimator is unbiased. A new untouched evaluation set or a properly justified simultaneous inference procedure is then needed.

Worked example 4: a lower bound is an expectation

Consider dates 0, 1 and 2 with zero interest. At date 1 an observed state is L or H with equal probability. Immediate exercise pays 5 in L and 1 in H. If held to date 2, a new independent fair coin gives 0 or 8 in L and 0 or 6 in H. No exercise at date 0 is permitted. Conditional continuation is 4 in L and 3 in H. The optimal rule exercises in L and waits in H, worth (5 + 3)/2 = 4.

A training fit that estimates continuation as 6 in L and 2 in H chooses to wait in both states. Its held-out expected value is (4 + 3)/2 = 3.5, a feasible-policy lower bound. Four independent evaluation paths could all be L with the high terminal coin, yielding an estimate of 8; this event has probability (1/4)4 = 1/256. “Lower bound” does not mean every sample mean is below 4. The hindsight strategy takes max(5, terminal payoff) in L and max(1, terminal payoff) in H. Its mean is [(.5·5 + .5·8) + (.5·1 + .5·6)]/2 = 5. That upper bound uses future coin outcomes and is not an exercisable trading policy.

7. Reproduce, intervene and report limits

Download the inputs, standard-library program, reference output, standalone instructions and four-file integrity manifest. Run python3 v10-c10-analysis.py --input v10-c10-inputs.json --output result.json; repeat with python3 -O. Importing the module or calling run(data) produces no console output and does not mutate data. The JSON domain excludes zero volatility/maturity and rejects unstable grids rather than inventing special-case results. Chapter 8 explains those financial boundary cases separately.

The CRR European puts at N = 24,48,96,192 are 11.682148, 11.652993, 11.619644 and 11.589741. The last estimate crosses the analytic price. Within each fixed tree, the European value is no greater than the put exercisable every fourth node date, which is no greater than the all-date value. At N = 192 these are 11.589741 ≤ 12.142317 ≤ 12.152470. No cross-N monotonicity is asserted. Parity checks the European call/put implementation independently of American exercise.

The checker recomputes terminal binomial sums, enumerates feasible small-tree policies, represents the PDE update as a killed random walk, integrates lognormal payoffs/moments directly, reconstructs sample summaries independently and tests meaningful financial interventions. It distinguishes checks against mathematical anchors from matching a saved JSON file. Hashes detect changed files; they do not prove financial validity. The README records the finite domain, generator protocol, per-estimator independent unit, bounded runtime and error limitations.

A model-use report should retain the contract, calibrated parameters and measure, input provenance, code and seed, units, stability and no-arbitrage checks, grid/domain comparisons, sampling uncertainty, independent benchmarks and unresolved limitations. If an estimate is used to invert volatility or compute Greeks, include those operations' conditioning. Chapter 11 adds claims and markets for which specifying numerical precision still leaves genuine pricing nonuniqueness.

8. Exercises

  1. Error and inverse conditioning. A European price calculation has a justified absolute error ≤ .012 CU. On the complete volatility bracket used for inversion, vega is at least 18 CU per unit σ. Bound the volatility error in absolute σ and percentage points. If central gamma uses a .20-CU spot bump and all three prices have error at most .012, bound the gamma error caused by price errors alone. Explain why neither result bounds model error.
  2. Tree transfer. In Worked example 1 change only the strike to 88. Compute all terminal put payoffs, both date-1 continuation values, decisions, European and all-date root prices. Check root immediate exercise. Give the exact early-exercise premium.
  3. Stopping proof and law changes. Prove the finite Snell recursion and the nested-exercise-set inequality. In a fixed N = 192 main-case tree compare exercise strides 192, 4 and 1. Explain why the all-date values at N = 24 and N = 192 need not have the same ordering. State the information error in pathwise hindsight maximization.
  4. Stencil and a counterexample. Take a = .02, b = .03, h = .10 and k = .20. Compute α, β, γ and check both positivity conditions. Apply one interior update to neighboring values (0,1,0). Repeat with k = .30 and exhibit the resulting violation of nonnegativity. Could making k smaller repair a spatial condition |b|h > 2a?
  5. Complete the numerical theorem. Under the regularity stated in Section 3, derive the constants 1/2, 1/12 and 1/6 in η, and prove the global ε + Tη bound. With T = 1, k = .001, h = .02, a = .02, |b| = .01, Mtt = 3, M4 = 20, M3 = 5 and ε = .0004, compute the bound. Identify the missing hypothesis if it is applied directly at a vanilla payoff kink.
  6. Boundary and refinement design. Two stable schemes have identical initial data and interior weights but boundary arrays differing by at most .006 in w-units. Let r = −.03 and T = 2. Bound their final option-price difference. A developer doubles L at fixed M, holding k unchanged; explain which error sources and positivity restrictions change, and design a useful domain comparison.
  7. Sampling guarantees. An iid discounted payoff lies in [0,50]. Find a sufficient integer sample size for absolute error at most .5 with probability at least .95 using the proved bound. If a preliminary independent variance estimate suggests standard deviation 8, compute the usual approximate 95% fixed-sample planning size for the same half-width. Explain the difference in guarantees and why checking every ten observations until a normal interval looks narrow changes the problem.
  8. Antithetic proof and failure. Prove the covariance identity in Section 5 and use it for a one-dimensional monotone put payoff. For f(z) = z2, compare the variance of n antithetic pair means with 2n independent evaluations, using EZ2 = 1 and EZ4 = 3. Explain the correct number of independent units in each case.
  9. Control coefficient and independence. Suppose Var Y = 100, Var X = 25 and Cov(Y,X) = −40, with EX known. Find the optimal coefficient, minimum variance and variances at βc = −1 and +1. Prove conditional unbiasedness for a coefficient selected from an independent pilot. Explain why the same-sample proof fails and why pairing may change the optimal coefficient.
  10. Exact GBM and bounded-payoff scope. Derive Lj by completing the normal square, then derive EY, EY2 and EYX for the put/discounted-stock control. Explain why exact terminal sampling removes Euler bias for a European put but not continuous-barrier monitoring bias. For a nonzero fixed stock-control coefficient, decide whether Yc remains bounded and whether the put Hoeffding interval applies.
  11. Policy evaluation. In Worked example 4, a frozen rule exercises in both date-1 states. Find its value and compare it with always waiting, the optimal rule and hindsight. Prove that an independently evaluated frozen rule has expectation at most the optimal finite-grid price. Give an explicit sample outcome refuting a pathwise lower-bound claim and explain what happens when the evaluation set is reused to select a rule.
  12. Numerical research critique. A report declares a continuously monitored American barrier claim accurate to .001 because two CRR prices differ by .0007. It also reports a Monte Carlo interval computed from all antithetic members as if independent, calibrates a control and an exercise rule on those same paths, and clips negative stencil weights. Design a reproducible correction and an acceptance decision. Include an independently checkable counterexample, a primary reading with its exact relevant scope, and separate evidence needed for pricing accuracy, policy quality and empirical model adequacy.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. Error amplification depends on the operation

    The inverse bound is .012/18 = .0006666667 in absolute σ, or .06666667 percentage points of volatility. This requires both compared volatilities to lie in the bracket over which vega has the stated lower bound. The three-price gamma numerator has coefficients (1,−2,1), so its worst price-error contribution is (1 + 2 + 1).012/.202 = 1.2 CU per CU2. This excludes the central-difference approximation error even for exact prices. Neither conclusion tests whether the diffusion, calibration or contract represents the market.

  2. Changing strike changes the exercise margin

    Terminal stocks remain 51.2,80,125; put payoffs are 36.8,8,0. At the down node continuation is [(7/15)36.8 + (8/15)8]/1.04 = 268/13 ≈ 20.615385; immediate exercise is 24, so exercise. At the up node continuation is [(7/15)8]/1.04 = 140/39 ≈ 3.589744; immediate exercise is zero, so continue. The European root is 16870/1521 ≈ 11.091387. Using 24 in the down branch gives the all-date root 19180/1521 ≈ 12.610125. Both exceed immediate root payoff 8. The exact premium is 2310/1521 = 770/507 ≈ 1.518738. It exceeds the original premium: at the down node intrinsic value rises by 4 while continuation rises by 4/1.04, so earlier receipt becomes more valuable.

  3. The feasible set proof keeps the law fixed

    At the final node V = g. Assume recursively that Vi+1 dominates every feasible later conditional value and that a later rule attains it. Any earlier rule either takes gi or waits with value at most the discounted conditional mean of Vi+1. Taking the maximum at permitted dates gives an upper bound that is attained by choosing the maximizing action and the already constructed later rule. At dates where exercise is forbidden only continuation is feasible. This proves the recursion by induction and its optimal stopping interpretation. Every rule on a subset of dates is also a rule on the larger set, so the supremum cannot fall.

    Stride 192 allows time 0 and maturity; the root intrinsic 4 is below European 11.589741071, so its value equals that European price. Stride 4 gives 12.142316804 and stride 1 gives 12.152470369. The inequality is within one probability tree. The all-date 24-step value 12.251137730 exceeds the 192-step value; refinement changed jumps and probabilities, so no nested-set argument orders them. Hindsight sees future movements when choosing a past date and is generally not a stopping time.

  4. A negative middle weight can create a negative price

    a/h2 = 2 and b/(2h) = .15. With k = .20, (α,β,γ) = (.37,.20,.43). The spatial condition .003 ≤ .04 and time condition .8 ≤ 1 hold. Updating (0,1,0) gives .20. At k = .30, weights are (.555,−.20,.645) and the same nonnegative data produce −.20. This counterexample disproves positivity, without relying on a long unstable run. If |b|h > 2a, one off-diagonal rate a/h2 ± b/(2h) is negative for every k > 0; a smaller k cannot fix its sign. Refine h or change the spatial discretization with a new consistency analysis.

  5. Local residuals accumulate through a stable operator

    In time, w(τ+k) = w + kwτ + ∫0k(k−s)wττ(τ+s)ds, so dividing the remainder by k gives kMtt/2. Spatial third-order Taylor expansions at x ± h, each with fourth-derivative remainder bounded by h4M4/24, add to give the second-difference error ≤ 2h4M4/(24h2) = h2M4/12. Second-order expansions with third-derivative remainder h3M3/6 subtract to give the first-difference error ≤ 2h3M3/(12h) = h2M3/6.

    Multiplying by a or |b| and by the time step k yields a residual at most kη. Error updates are convex combinations plus that residual; including new boundary values gives Em+1 ≤ max(ε,Em+kη). Starting from E0 ≤ ε proves Em ≤ ε+mkη and hence the claim. Numerically η = .0015 + .000013333333 + .000003333333 = .001516666667. The global bound is .001916666667 in w-units. The raw payoff kink lacks the bounded continuous spatial derivatives required on the closed rectangle, and the time derivative bounds can also fail at zero remaining time.

  6. A domain comparison needs comparable resolution

    The discrete maximum principle gives a w difference no greater than .006. Price difference is at most e.06.006 = .00637101928 CU. This bounds only the two numerical boundary treatments, not their common mesh error or distance to the desired full-domain solution. Doubling L at fixed M doubles h: spatial truncation terms can grow fourfold, the central-drift condition becomes harder to satisfy, and the explicit time condition becomes easier because k/h2 shrinks. A useful comparison doubles L and M together to preserve h, uses the same k, checks that the strike and requested spot remain correctly located, and then separately refines h and k. For a total bound one still needs justified boundary accuracy and the relevant solution regularity.

  7. A conservative guarantee and an approximate plan

    Require n ≥ B2log(2/.05)/(2ε2) = 2500log40/.5 ≈ 18444.39727, so 18445 suffices. Using standard deviation 8 in a normal planning formula gives n ≥ (1.959963985·8/.5)2 ≈ 983.413458, so 984. The first is a finite-sample bound under independent bounded observations; it ignores the smaller variance. The second uses an estimated variance and asymptotic normal approximation, so it is a planning calculation, not a .95 coverage guarantee. Repeatedly inspecting and stopping on an estimated width makes the stopping time depend on the observations and invalidates the fixed-n argument without further sequential analysis. Independent pilot planning followed by a fixed main sample preserves a clearer conditional design but does not make normal coverage exact.

  8. Count the pairs

    Expanding the product for independent Z,Z′ gives two copies of E[g(Z)h(Z)] and subtracts two copies of Eg·Eh, proving the identity. A decreasing put payoff and its reflected increasing function have pairwise differences of opposite signs, so covariance is nonpositive. Dividing their summed variance by 4 and averaging n independent pairs proves the stated improvement relative to 2n independent observations.

    For z2, Var f(Z) = 3 − 1 = 2. Reflection changes nothing, so a pair mean is Z2; n independent pairs give variance 2/n. A mean of 2n independent squared normals has variance 1/n. Thus pairing is twice as variable for equal payoff evaluations. The pair is one independent unit; dependence inside a pair cannot be erased by calling its two values separate samples.

  9. A signed coefficient is a financial decision

    βc* = −40/25 = −1.6. Minimum variance is 100 − 1600/25 = 36. At −1 it is 100 + 25 − 80 = 45; at +1 it is 100 + 25 + 80 = 205. The sign mistake more than doubles the original variance. Conditional on an independent pilot A, β̂(A) is fixed and E[X̄ | A] = EX, so E[Ȳ − β̂(A)(X̄−EX) | A] = EY. Integrability of the coefficient-adjusted estimator is needed to average this identity over pilots; a bounded fitted coefficient suffices. With same-sample fitting, β̂ and X̄ are dependent, so the product's expectation cannot be factorized. Pair means define new Y and X observations with new covariances; reusing −1.6 need not minimize their variance.

  10. Exact transitions and moment identities have a precise scope

    Write ST = exp(m+wZ), m = log S+(r−q−σ2/2)T and w = σ√T. The event is Z < c = (log K−m)/w. The integrand for Lj contains exp(jm+jwz)φ(z). Completing the exponent gives exp(jm+j2w2/2)φ(z−jw); its integral to c is that prefactor times Φ(c−jw), precisely the formula in Section 5. Expanding (K−ST)1{ST<K}, its square, and its product with ST yields the three displayed moments after applying D or D2.

    The exact terminal GBM law directly generates a European payoff, so there is no Euler step. A continuous barrier concerns whether a crossing occurred between observation times; knowing the endpoint law or even exact discrete transitions does not answer that event. A separate bridge or monitoring correction needs justification. If βc ≠ 0, on large ST the put is zero while −βc(DST−m) grows without a finite two-sided bound. Hence the bounded-put Hoeffding formula is not valid for the adjusted observation. Finite variance still holds under GBM.

  11. Policy quality and sampling noise are separate

    Always exercising at date 1 gives (5 + 1)/2 = 3; always waiting gives 3.5; optimal adapted exercise gives 4; hindsight gives 5. For any frozen training result A, its feasible rule belongs to the set over which Vgrid takes a supremum, proving E[discounted receipt | A] ≤ Vgrid. Independent evaluation observations have this conditional mean; averaging over training data preserves the inequality. Always-exercise evaluation paths that are all L have sample value 5, exceeding 4 with probability 2−n. Worked example 4 supplies another counterexample for the waiting rule. Selecting the largest evaluated mean uses positive noise in the choice; the old evaluation set no longer supports the same unbiased selected-policy claim. Freeze selection and obtain fresh independent evaluation.

  12. A defensible correction needs several distinct experiments

    A strong report first fixes contractual exercise dates, barrier direction, monitoring, rebate/payment timing, stock model and calibration measure. It rejects invalid tree probabilities or stencil weights and reports the actual stability conditions; the (0,1,0) update yielding −.20 in Exercise 4 is a direct counterexample to the clipping-based logic. Clipping changes the operator and its consistency, so even a stable clipped scheme needs a new target and analysis. Two nearby CRR prices can share bias or oscillate around a limit; their difference is not an error bound.

    Then compare an analytic European anchor and an independent small-tree policy enumeration; vary domain, space/time and exercise/monitoring resolution separately under clearly stated laws; and report the absence of a proven continuous-barrier/American convergence bound if none is available. Use pair means for antithetic standard errors. Freeze controls and exercise rules using training/pilot data, evaluate on fresh paths, and distinguish a feasible-policy expectation lower bound from a sample bound. A dual upper certificate would require an independently justified construction; hindsight supplies only a potentially loose bound.

    For primary context, Haugh's variance-reduction notes Sections 2–3 concern controls, pair means and cost/variance comparisons, while the stopping paper Section 2.1 concerns approximate continuation rules and their policy values; neither citation certifies this report's barrier implementation. Retain data/code/seed/version, unit tests with mathematical oracles, failure cases, tolerances and a holdout plan. Acceptance should be limited to contracts and errors actually supported by evidence; with the stated evidence, the .001 accuracy claim must be rejected. Independent market observations, executable conventions and out-of-sample pricing/hedging evidence are required for empirical adequacy. Grade 2 points each for target/error separation, valid numerical diagnostics, correct sampling units, training/evaluation separation, and scoped evidence/acceptance reasoning; a polished report without an adapted exercise rule does not pass.

9. Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back prompt. Explain to a colleague why a stable PDE grid, an exact GBM transition, and a narrow Monte Carlo interval can all coexist with a wrong American barrier price.

Model answer. Stability controls the propagation of perturbations for a declared discretization; it does not identify its boundary data or contractual target. Exact transitions sample the chosen stock process at chosen dates; they do not reveal an intervening barrier crossing. A Monte Carlo interval measures sampling error for the implemented payoff/policy under ideal independent draws. American exercise must use current information, and a learned feasible rule still has an optimality gap. All three computational properties can hold while monitoring, policy, market model or contract specification is wrong. A complete explanation connects each claimed diagnostic to its actual estimand rather than listing methods.

Retention check, after a week without the code. (1) With b = 0, a = .05 and h = .1, what is the largest positive explicit k allowed by the maximum-principle condition? (2) A Monte Carlo standard error is .12 at 2500 iid observations; how many observations approximately halve it? (3) Why does a feasible-policy lower bound not make each simulation estimate a lower bound? (4) What derivative hypotheses block immediate use of the smooth PDE error theorem for a vanilla payoff?

Answers. (1) k ≤ h2/(2a) = .1, with boundary data included in the maximum principle. (2) Four times as many, 10000, under unchanged observation variance and independent sampling; this says nothing about bias. (3) The policy's expected discounted payoff is bounded by the supremum; its finite-sample mean has noise of either sign, as the explicit 5-CU and 8-CU examples show. (4) Uniform bounded continuous wττ, wxxx and wxxxx on the closed rectangle are not supplied by a kinked τ = 0 payoff. Remediate a missed answer by rederiving the corresponding inequality, then use new parameters.

10. Sources and further study

Primary readings are Mike Giles, Introduction to finite difference methods, slides 4–8; Martin Haugh, Output Analysis and Run-Length Control, Sections 1–2; Haugh, Simulation Efficiency and an Introduction to Variance Reduction, Sections 2–3; and Haugh, Duality Theory and Simulation in Financial Engineering (2003), Section 2.1. They provide method context; the cases, programs, proofs and problems above are original. Source-body inspection is distinct from independent review of this package.

Further study should prove weak convergence and uniform integrability for tree payoffs, optimal-stopping convergence, nonsmooth PDE error estimates, positivity-preserving implicit schemes, multilevel and randomized quasi-Monte Carlo, bridge corrections for barriers, and regression/dual stopping guarantees. None of these broader theories is claimed to follow merely from the experiments supplied here.

Sources and further study

  • Mike Giles — Lecture 1: Introduction to finite difference methods (AIMS lecture notes) — Primary teaching context for the forward-time central-space heat stencil, explicit time restriction and maximum-norm stability argument. The chapter independently derives its discounted log-price drift scheme and conditional smooth-solution error bound.
  • Martin Haugh — Output Analysis and Run-Length Control (2017) — Primary source context for iid sample means, variance, approximate CLT intervals and fixed/pilot run-length planning. The chapter proves its own bounded-payoff concentration bound and carefully separates a fixed-sample guarantee from sequential stopping.
  • Martin Haugh — Simulation Efficiency and an Introduction to Variance Reduction Methods — Primary method context for cost-times-variance comparisons, independent-pilot controls, antithetic pair units and their covariance criterion. Chapter derives signed controls and a one-dimensional non-strict covariance inequality with original numerical cases.
  • Martin Haugh — Duality Theory and Simulation in Financial Engineering (Proceedings of the 2003 Winter Simulation Conference) — Primary research context for regression continuation approximations, feasible adapted exercise policies, and further study of dual bounds. The chapter proves only finite-grid optimal stopping and independent fixed-policy expected lower bounds, not the paper's full duality theory.
